dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: Tell me about a time when you had to adapt quickly in your job.

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: When I started at the NGO, my manager left after two weeks. I had to take over her responsibilities immediately. Although I hadn't managed a team before, I organised a meeting, listed all the tasks, and divided them clearly. By the end of the month, we had met all our targets.

dialogue.speaker: Interviewer
dialogue.text: What did you learn from that experience?

dialogue.speaker: Daniyar
dialogue.text: That structure reduces anxiety. When everything is listed and assigned, the situation becomes manageable even when it is difficult.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: I've been reading about income inequality in Central Asia. The gap between urban and rural incomes has widened significantly over the past decade.

dialogue.speaker: Bekzod
dialogue.text: I know. And the consequences aren't just economic. Access to quality education and healthcare is highly unequal. As a result, social mobility has become much more difficult for rural populations.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: Although government spending on education has increased, the distribution is still concentrated in cities. Furthermore, many rural teachers are underpaid and underqualified.

dialogue.speaker: Bekzod
dialogue.text: Nevertheless, there are examples of NGOs working effectively in rural areas — training teachers, providing digital resources, supporting local communities. These initiatives are small, but they demonstrate what is possible.

dialogue.speaker: Zara
dialogue.text: What strikes me is that the people most affected by inequality are also the least likely to have their voices heard in policy discussions. That's the deepest problem.

dialogue.speaker: Bekzod
dialogue.text: Agreed. Crucially, addressing inequality requires not just resources but genuine inclusion — ensuring that affected communities are part of designing the solutions.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Good afternoon. I want to talk today about three ways in which technology is reshaping the world of work — and what this means for the skills we will need in the coming decade.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Firstly, automation. Many routine tasks — in manufacturing, data processing, and even some areas of professional services — are being performed by machines. As a result, workers who perform only routine tasks face an uncertain future. This is not new. But the speed of change is accelerating.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Secondly, remote and digital collaboration. The pandemic accelerated a shift that was already underway: the move from fixed-location work to flexible, distributed teams. Consequently, communication skills — particularly in writing and in cross-cultural contexts — have become more valuable, not less.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: Thirdly, and perhaps most importantly, the rise of AI tools that augment human work. These tools are not replacing human judgement — they are changing what human judgement needs to focus on. Crucially, the workers who will thrive are those who can work effectively alongside these tools, directing them, evaluating their outputs, and applying the contextual understanding that machines cannot replicate.

dialogue.speaker: Speaker
dialogue.text: The upshot is this: the future belongs to adaptable, communicatively skilled, critically thinking workers. Investing in language, reasoning, and intercultural competence is not optional — it is strategic.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Asel
dialogue.text: Today I want to examine the tension between individual action and collective responsibility in addressing environmental problems.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: Professor, isn't individual action important? If everyone reduced their carbon footprint, the impact would be significant.

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Asel
dialogue.text: That's a reasonable position, Amir. Nevertheless, research suggests that individual choices account for a relatively small share of total emissions compared to industrial and systemic sources. The most significant reductions require policy change, not individual lifestyle adjustment alone.

dialogue.speaker: Kamila
dialogue.text: But doesn't individual action have indirect effects — signalling to governments and companies what citizens want?

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Asel
dialogue.text: Absolutely. And this is where the debate becomes nuanced. Individual action matters as a signal and as a norm-setter. But it cannot substitute for structural change. Insofar as we focus exclusively on individual behaviour, we risk letting industrial emitters avoid accountability.

dialogue.speaker: Amir
dialogue.text: So the answer is both — but in the right proportion?

dialogue.speaker: Prof. Asel
dialogue.text: Precisely. By virtue of their scale and systemic impact, governments and corporations bear a greater share of responsibility. Individual action, however, builds the social foundation that makes political change possible.

questions.text: "___ he hadn't managed a team before, he organised the work effectively." (concession — clause)
questions.correct: Although
questions.hint: "Although + clause (subject + verb)" = concessive conjunction. ✅

questions.text: "___ the government spending, the distribution is still unequal." (concession — noun)
questions.correct: Despite
questions.hint: "Despite + noun/gerund" — no separate clause. ✅

questions.text: "Communication skills have become more important. ___, companies are investing more in training."
questions.correct: As a result / Therefore / Consequently
questions.hint: Cause → effect: THEREFORE / AS A RESULT / CONSEQUENTLY. ✅

questions.text: "Routine tasks ___ (perform) by machines now." (passive — ongoing)
questions.correct: are being performed
questions.hint: "Are being performed" = Present Continuous Passive. ✅

questions.text: "By virtue of ___ scale, corporations bear greater responsibility." Correct form:
questions.correct: their
questions.hint: "By virtue of THEIR scale" — plural possessive. ✅

questions.text: "___ we focus exclusively on individual behaviour, we risk letting emitters avoid accountability."
questions.correct: Insofar as
questions.hint: "Insofar as + clause" = to the degree that. ✅

questions.text: "She told me that the report ___ submitted the previous day." (reported — past passive)
questions.correct: had been submitted
questions.hint: "Had been submitted" = Past Perfect Passive in reported speech. ✅

questions.text: "Crucially, the workers who ___ ___ alongside AI tools will thrive." (work — relative)
questions.correct: can work
questions.hint: "Workers who can work alongside AI tools" = relative clause with modal. ✅

questions.correct: Able to be handled without too much difficulty

questions.text: "AI tools augment human work." "Augment" means:
opts: Enhance or add to the capability of
questions.correct: Enhance or add to the capability of
questions.hint: "augment" = to add to or improve; to make greater.

questions.text: "Letting emitters avoid accountability." "Accountability" means:
opts: Being responsible and answerable for actions
questions.correct: Being responsible and answerable for actions
questions.hint: "accountability" = the obligation to answer for your actions and their consequences.

questions.text: "Social mobility has become more difficult." "Social mobility" means:
opts: The ability to move between social classes through education or work
questions.correct: The ability to move between social classes through education or work
questions.hint: "social mobility" = the ability to improve your social position — upward or downward.

questions.text: "The upshot is this: adaptable workers will thrive." "Upshot" means:
questions.correct: The final result or conclusion
questions.hint: "the upshot" = the final result; what everything adds up to. Informal but common in spoken presentations.
